title: Managing conversation context
notes: The context window is large, but every token you send costs money and time, and every call resends the chat.
Keep long chats lean: trim old turns, summarise what you trim, and pin key facts like the order number.
Trim at whole customer turns, so a tool call is never separated from its result.

slides.title: Managing conversation context
slides.sub: Keep long chats fast and affordable without losing what matters
sentences: In the last lesson, short-term memory meant sending the conversation again with every call.
That works beautifully for ten messages.
In this lesson you will see what happens at forty, and three simple ways to keep a long chat fast, cheap and on track.

slides.title: The context window
slides.definition: The most a model can read and write in one call, counted in tokens: system prompt, tools, messages and reply.

analogy.label: Think of it as
analogy.text: A desk. A huge desk holds plenty of paper, but every sheet on it still has to be read before you answer.

sentences: First, a term you will hear a lot: the context window.
It's the most text a model can handle in one call, counted in tokens. A token is roughly three quarters of a word.
It covers everything: the system prompt, the tool definitions, the messages, and the reply itself.
Claude Opus 5.5 has a context window of one million tokens, enough for several long novels.
Think of it as a desk. A huge desk holds plenty, but every sheet on it still has to be read before you answer.

slides.title: A long chat gets heavier every turn

note.text: Opus 5.5 input costs $4 per million tokens. More input also means a slower reply.

sentences: Big isn't free, though, because every call sends the whole conversation again.
Say each turn adds about five hundred tokens. The first call sends five hundred.
By turn ten, each call sends five thousand tokens.
By turn forty, it's twenty thousand tokens per call, for a single customer.
Add up all forty calls and you have sent over four hundred thousand tokens, about one dollar sixty, just for input.
And more input means a slower reply, because the model has to read it all before it writes a word.

slides.title: Three ways to keep context lean

cards.title: Summarise
flow: The gist in a few lines

cards.title: Pin key facts
flow: Copy facts to a small dict

sentences: There are three simple techniques, and good agents combine them.
Trim: send only the last few turns, say the last ten.
It's simple and cheap, but anything older falls out, which is exactly what happened to Ravi.
Summarise: when the chat gets long, ask the model to condense the older turns into a short note.
You keep the gist, but a summary can quietly drop a detail.
Pin key facts: copy the details that must never be lost, like the order number, into a small list.
Pinned facts go into the system prompt on every call, however old they are.

slides.title: What Scout sends on message twenty-two

note.text: A small request, and the order number can't fall out.

sentences: Here's what a well-built request looks like on Ravi's twenty-second message.
First, in the system prompt, the pinned facts: his order number and his name.
Next, a short summary of the older turns, written by the model a while back.
Then the last ten messages, word for word, so the recent back and forth is exact.
Scout gets everything it needs, and nothing it doesn't.
The request stays small, and the order number can never fall out.

slides.title: Trim at whole turns
slides.lead: Cut only where a customer turn begins, so a tool call is never split from its result.

rows.out: pinned facts added on every call

aside.label: The trap
aside.text: Cut by message count and you may keep a tool result but drop its tool call. The API rejects that.

sentences: Trimming sounds easy: keep the last ten messages. There's one trap.
First, find where each customer turn begins: a message the customer actually typed, not a list of tool results.
Then keep everything from the tenth-last turn onward.
If you cut by message count instead, you can keep a tool result but drop the tool call it answers, and the API rejects the request.
Finally, add the pinned facts to the system prompt, so they ride along with every call.

slides.title: Summarising in practice
slides.scenario: Ravi's chat passes 30 turns. The oldest 20 are condensed into a short note.

steps.text: The chat passes the limit; the oldest 20 turns are set aside
A small model writes: Ravi, ORB-10533, asked about mat size and returns
The note replaces 20 turns; facts and the last 10 messages stay
Scout keeps the gist at a fraction of the tokens

result.text: One cheap summary call saves tokens on every call that follows.

sentences: Here's summarising in practice.
Ravi's chat passes thirty turns, so the code sets aside the oldest twenty.
It makes one extra call, often to a small, cheap model like Haiku, asking for the gist in a few lines.
That note replaces the twenty turns, while the pinned facts and the recent messages stay as they are.
From then on, Scout carries the early chat at a fraction of the tokens.
One cheap summary call pays for itself on every call that follows.

slides.title: What to take away

points.text: The context window is large, but every token costs money and time.
Every call resends the chat, so long chats get slower and pricier.
Trim old turns, summarise them, and pin key facts.
Trim at whole turns so tool calls keep their results.

sentences: Let's recap.
The context window is huge, but it isn't free: every token costs money and time.
Because every call resends the conversation, a long chat gets heavier with each turn.
Trim old turns, summarise what you trim, and pin the facts that must never be lost.
When you trim, cut at whole customer turns, so a tool call never loses its result.
Next, Scout learns to look things up in Orbit's own documents.

midQuiz.q: Why does call forty of a chat cost more than call four?
options: Long conversations are billed at a higher rate
Each call resends the whole conversation as input
Long chats are switched to a bigger model
midQuiz.explain: The API keeps nothing between calls, so every call carries the full history. More history means more input tokens, and more cost.
midQuiz.hint: What does each call have to include for the model to know the chat so far?

midQuiz.q: Which technique keeps Ravi's order number in view however long the chat gets?
options: Trimming to the last ten messages
Pinning it as a fact in the system prompt
Moving to a model with a bigger context window
midQuiz.explain: Pinned facts are added to the system prompt on every call, so trimming old messages can't remove them.
midQuiz.hint: Which technique adds something to every call, however old it is?

endQuiz.q: Priya trims Scout's history to the last 8 messages by count, and the API sometimes rejects the request. Why?
options: Eight messages is below the API's minimum
The cut can keep a tool result but drop the tool call it answers
Trimmed chats must be summarised first
endQuiz.explain: A tool result must follow the assistant message that asked for it. Cutting at whole customer turns keeps each pair together.
endQuiz.hint: Think about what a tool result needs right before it.

endQuiz.q: What is the main risk of summarising old turns?
options: The summary can quietly drop a detail that mattered
Summaries make every later call slower
The model can't read a summary in the prompt
endQuiz.explain: A summary keeps the gist, not every detail. That is why key facts like the order number are pinned separately.
endQuiz.hint: What does a summary give up in exchange for being short?
